idiom_name: private instance fields of the smallest owning class; method locals for transient values
implementation_notes: Java realizes the pattern with plain encapsulation: declare the state as private fields of the smallest class that reads it - a panel, controller or small state holder - and keep transient values in method locals, so the value's lifetime and visibility are exactly the owner's. The replacement for the classic structure is this field-in-the-owner arrangement: a static field or an application-scoped singleton is the Java shape of a global store, and it should be reserved for state that is genuinely application-wide (configuration, session registries, caches). When two views must observe the same value, move it to their closest common owner - a shared controller or model object - rather than to a static; classic static state remains justified for process-wide constants and genuinely process-wide services, not for per-screen UI state.
pitfalls: A static field is JVM-wide and shared by every user and screen (in server-side UIs, across sessions); per-screen state placed in a static is the classic Java over-lift.
Swing/JavaFX component state must be touched on the UI thread (EDT or FX application thread); state colocated in a component that a worker thread mutates is a race even though the field is private.
Lambdas and anonymous inner classes capture the enclosing component strongly, so a listener registered on a long-lived publisher keeps the whole panel alive after the screen is closed.
